reports.name: Shohei Ohtani
reports.published_report: The xwOBA splits say everything: .415 as a hitter, .257 as a pitcher, both sitting at the 95th percentile or better in their respective directions. That's not a curiosity — it's two legitimate starting-caliber profiles sharing one body. The bat carries 93.6 mph average exit velocity and a 15.3% walk rate into a projection of 38 home runs and a .946 OPS over 691 plate appearances, while the arm runs 98.1 mph with a 2.70 xERA and a 30.4% whiff rate. The one thing worth watching: pitching control sits at a 7.6% walk rate, and the chase numbers on both sides of the ball are closer to league-average than the power metrics suggest, so the ceiling on the mound hinges on whether he can tighten the zone command as his Dodger workload builds.

reports.name: Junior Caminero
reports.published_report: Forty-six home runs projected at age 22, and the contact quality is already there to believe it: 93.3 mph average exit velocity and a 51.5% hard-hit rate sit at the 95th and 92nd percentiles respectively, and the .371 xwOBA says the underlying skill is ahead of what his current line shows. The discipline is quieter but meaningful, a 12.7% walk rate against a 17.9% strikeout rate that together make a .909 OPS season look sustainable rather than lucky. He is not going to beat you with his legs, and the fielding data is as bad as it gets, so the profile lives or dies on whether the bat stays this loud. If it does, he's a genuine middle-of-the-order force; if the contact shape erodes as pitchers adjust, what's left is a slow corner bat without the glove to compensate.

reports.name: Bobby Witt Jr.
reports.published_report: The xBA sits at .314, 100th percentile, and the projected .293 AVG is almost conservative by comparison. Witt's contact quality is genuine across every dimension: 93.3 mph average exit velocity, 53.5% hard-hit rate, an xSLG of .529, all clustering in the 95th percentile, which is why a projection of 24 home runs and 47 stolen bases at shortstop reads as a floor more than a ceiling. The one real friction in the profile is a 33.0% chase rate, well below average, and if pitchers ever find a consistent way to exploit it the strikeout rate climbs from its current manageable 16.6%. That's the dependency: everything downstream of the contact quality holds as long as the chase rate doesn't become a true weapon against him.

reports.name: Pete Crow-Armstrong
reports.published_report: The xwOBA (.366) and hard-hit rate (49.6%) are doing real work here, because the chase rate (36.4%) keeps setting off alarms that the contact numbers don't fully justify. Crow-Armstrong is putting the ball in the air hard enough, often enough, that the 25.4% strikeout rate looks more manageable than it sounds, and the sprint speed at the 95th percentile means every single and every stolen-base opportunity gets squeezed for maximum value. If the chase rate stays where it is and pitchers learn to attack it more systematically, the .276 projection holds only if the hard contact holds with it. Thirty-one home runs and 38 steals at 24 is the kind of profile that doesn't need the plate discipline to be pretty, it needs it to be good enough, and right now it just barely clears that bar.

reports.name: Nick Kurtz
reports.published_report: The contact hasn't caught up to the power yet, and it may never fully close — but at 23, Kurtz doesn't need it to. His 94.4 mph average exit velocity and 18.7% barrel rate sit at the very top of the league, and an 18.9% walk rate that leads all of baseball means pitchers who try to avoid the damage are just feeding a different problem. The 31.3% strikeout rate is the hinge: if he sharpens contact within the zone, the .386 xwOBA becomes a floor; if the 36.4% whiff rate proves sticky, he's a three-true-outcomes first baseman with elite upside rather than a true middle-of-the-order anchor. The projection calling for 37 home runs and a .400 OBP in a full season isn't a stretch given what the contact quality already shows, just waiting on a 23-year-old to figure out the last piece.

reports.name: Yordan Alvarez
reports.published_report: The xwOBA is .474 and the xSLG is .712, both at the 100th percentile, which means there's no peer group at this level, just Alvarez and then everyone else. A 19.1% barrel rate with 53.8% hard contact and a 14.9% walk rate means pitchers have no clean path to him: challenge him and he does damage, avoid him and he takes the base. The projection, .310/.417/1.022 with 45 home runs in 675 plate appearances, reads like a reasonable translation of that Statcast profile, not an optimistic one. The one thing working against him is the one thing that can't change: he's slow enough to be a full-time DH, so if the bat ever cools, there's no glove or speed to absorb it.

reports.name: Paul Skenes
reports.published_report: The xERA sits at 2.76 and the K% at 30.1, and those two numbers together say the same thing: the stuff is translating into results the way you'd expect it to. The profile is built on strikeouts and control, not on limiting hard contact, which is fine when the 5.6% walk rate keeps the whiff-or-damage dynamic off the table. The projection calls for a 3.31 ERA over 179.17 innings, and the gap between that and the 2.76 xERA is mostly about regression to the contact side, where his barrel and hard-hit numbers run closer to league average than his strikeout numbers suggest. If the command holds and the innings accumulate, this is a legitimate top-of-rotation arm at 23; if workload management clips the IP total or the walk rate creeps, you're still looking at a very good pitcher, just a shorter one.

reports.name: Fernando Tatis Jr.
reports.published_report: The hard contact is legitimate and the xBA tells you why: a .284 xBA at the 90th percentile means pitchers aren't beating him with weak contact, they're beating him with whiffs. A 28.6% whiff rate drags the .430 xSLG into something more pedestrian, and the projection lands accordingly at .419 SLG, real production, not a power profile. What he gives back with the bat he partially reclaims with his legs; 35 projected steals on 29.0 ft/s sprint speed is a genuine weapon, and the 52.9% hard-hit rate means when he does connect, outfielders are moving. The profile hinges on whether he can tighten the zone enough to let that exit velocity play up: if the whiff rate holds, you get a useful everyday player who tops out around .768 OPS; if he starts punishing mistakes more consistently, the .350 xwOBA points toward something better.

reports.name: Corbin Carroll
reports.published_report: The Statcast profile here is quietly lopsided in a useful way. Carroll's contact side is ordinary, a 29.1% whiff rate that bleeds expected batting average down to .258, but everything he squares up grades well, with a 91.4 mph average exit velocity and a 46.7% hard-hit rate that together explain why xwOBA (.350) and xSLG (.455) both land comfortably above average. Add a sprint speed at the 96th percentile and an 11.3% walk rate, and the projection's .848 OPS with 25 home runs and 21 stolen bags over 675 plate appearances has a real mechanical foundation. The whole profile hinges on whether the whiff rate stays manageable, because if it climbs, the contact outcomes get uglier fast and the power isn't so overwhelming that it covers a true strikeout problem. He's a legitimate everyday center fielder with a plus run dimension, and if the swing-and-miss tightens even a little, the ceiling is an above-average regular with multi-category value at scale.

reports.published_report: The contact grade is doing the heavy lifting here, and the 19 steals in 349 PA give him a profile that's actually interesting. His K rate translates to 18% against big-league arms, four points below the average hitter faces, and he's drawing walks at a clip that converts to 9.5% in MLB context. reports.name: CJ Abrams
reports.published_report: Thirty home runs from a shortstop who runs a 37.1% chase rate is the whole tension in this profile. The contact quality is quietly solid, a 10.0% barrel rate and .336 xwOBA both sitting comfortably above the middle of the league, which is what makes the chase number so frustrating — there's genuine damage in the bat when he connects, but he's giving pitchers an easy road to avoid the barrel. Speed is legitimate, 28.4 ft/s, and that plus the pop is what gets you to a .818 OPS projection across 660 PA at short. If the chase rate stays where it is, the strikeout load stays manageable enough at 21.7% and the production holds; if pitchers keep expanding him successfully and he can't make an adjustment, the .251 xBA is the floor that shows through.

reports.name: Sal Stewart
reports.published_report: The 14.9% barrel rate is doing real work here, 91st percentile, and it shows up in the xSLG (.478, 83rd percentile) more than in the raw hard-hit numbers, which means the damage is concentrated rather than broad. The 28.0% whiff rate sits in the 32nd percentile, and that's the tension: the contact Stewart makes is better than most hitters in the league, but he doesn't make it as often as you'd like from a corner. What saves the profile is an 11.4% walk rate pulling the OBP off the floor, and at 22 the projection, .256/.337/.457 with 28 home runs, looks like a solid second-division regular with a path to more if the whiff rate tightens even modestly. If it doesn't, he's a high-damage platoon piece who earns his spot on a lineup card but doesn't anchor one.

Hitters are swinging at his stuff out of the zone at an elite clip, which explains both the 4.8% walk rate and the 32.3% whiff rate. He's not winning with power or stuff quality; he's winning with location and deception, and the contact numbers confirm it: 44.1% hard-hit and a 9.0% barrel rate that sits in the bottom third of the league haven't hurt him because he's not giving hitters clean looks at pitches they can drive. reports.name: Chase Burns
reports.published_report: The 2607 rpm fastball spin is doing real work here — pair that with 97.8 mph and you have a reason the 32.8% whiff rate and 29.7 K% aren't accidents of small sample. Burns is generating chases at a 34.8% clip and the contact quality numbers, while not elite, sit comfortably in average range, which is what you'd expect when hitters are mostly late or missing entirely. The one honest limitation is command: a 7.9 BB% lands below average and is the pressure point in the profile, because if the walks climb, the strikeout margin stops covering them. If he tightens that number even modestly, a projected 2.92 ERA across a full starter's workload puts him squarely in frontline conversation; if the walks stay where they are, he's still a useful mid-rotation arm who misses enough bats to survive it.

reports.name: Bryce Harper
reports.published_report: The xwOBA (.404) and xSLG (.540) are both in the 97th percentile, and neither number requires explanation — the 14.9% walk rate does the work of keeping pitchers honest, and when they attack him, 47.2% of contact qualifies as hard-hit. The tension is that a 30.5% whiff rate and 33.6% chase rate sit well below average for a hitter generating these expected outcomes, meaning the actual line (.270/.373/.509, per the projection) reflects a contact profile that costs him a few points of batting average his quality of contact probably deserves. Fielding is essentially not a skill he offers anymore, so his value lives entirely in the bat, and that bat projects to 33 home runs and an .882 OPS across 677 plate appearances. At 33, with that shape, you're buying a dangerous middle-of-the-order presence who walks more than almost anyone and hits the ball hard enough to survive the swing-and-miss.

reports.name: Josh Naylor
reports.published_report: The xBA sits at .271 while exit velocity checks in at 87.5 mph — that gap is the whole Naylor puzzle. He makes contact at an elite rate, 12.7% strikeouts against a chase rate of 37.0% that should crater that number but somehow doesn't, because he puts wood on nearly everything he swings at. The power, though, is genuinely soft: a 4.9% barrel rate and 37.1% hard-hit rate translate to a projected .390 SLG, and there's no Statcast shape hiding a coming breakout. What he actually is: a plus contact profile squeezed into a below-average power frame at first base, saved partly by 23 projected stolen bases that make the .710 OPS play better in counting stats than it looks on paper. If the contact holds and the speed ages gracefully, he's a useful regular; if the chase rate finally catches up with him, you're left with a slow first baseman who doesn't hit the ball hard.

reports.name: Ceddanne Rafaela
reports.published_report:
The Statcast profile is almost entirely below-average contact quality, and the projection still has him hitting .271 with 22 steals. That tension is the whole read.

At 86.0 mph average exit velocity and a 33.1% hard-hit rate, Rafaela makes weak contact at a rate that would bury most hitters. What saves the projection is that his 20.1% strikeout rate is near league average, meaning he puts the ball in play enough to let his sprint speed, sitting at the 91st percentile, do the work. His .286 xwOBA and 5.0% walk rate are ceilings on his offensive upside, so if his batted-ball luck regresses or his 40.3% chase rate gets exploited more aggressively, the hit tool evaporates and you're left with a spectacular defender who bats eighth. The floor is a glove-first fourth outfielder; if the contact rates hold and the legs keep producing, he's a second-division regular with stolen-base value baked in.

reports.published_report: Eighteen home runs and a .535 slugging percentage in 331 AAA plate appearances, with a .232 ISO that translates to around .172 against MLB pitching — that's a real power number, even after the level discount. The hit tool is doing work too: a .303 average against AAA arms, and the contact-over-walk approach shows up clearly in a BB% that lands essentially at the big-league mean while the strikeout rate sits a few ticks above it. If the bat plays up, he's a low-end everyday third baseman; if the strikeouts spike, he's a right-handed bench bat who can punish a mistake.

reports.name: AJ Russell
reports.peak_summary: Projection: depth arm with high risk. The current pitching shape is limited over 26.7 IP.
reports.published_report: The strikeout stuff is legitimate noise — 14.0 K/9 across A and A+ this year, a 98th-percentile K-BB% among arms with 20-plus innings in this pool. But the shape has a crack in it. Translate the profile to a major-league context and the walk rate lands at 4.0 per nine, a full tick above the league average, which means the 80-grade miss is doing a lot of work that 50-grade command may not be able to sustain. Over 35.4 innings the ERA and WHIP look clean, but the projection isn't buying a rotation future: the ceiling here is a useful MLB arm, with the floor a bullpen piece, and the two-to-three-year clock gives the command room to develop or expose itself. If the walks tighten, there's a real weapon somewhere in this profile; if they don't, the strikeouts become relief-only goods.

reports.name: Jackson Kent
reports.peak_summary: Projection: multi-inning or setup reliever with medium risk. The current pitching shape is bat missing over 38 IP.
reports.published_report: The walk rate is the argument here. Across 68.7 IP split between AA and AAA, Kent has issued just 20 walks, a 2.6 BB/9 that translates to roughly 3.0 against MLB hitters, a tick below the big-league average. His K-BB% of 22% against this competition becomes a translated 15.3%, which clears the major-league mean of 13.5%, so the command is doing real work even after the level discount. The shape that emerges is a reliever who controls the zone well enough to hold a high-leverage spot, with a 50-grade miss tool that makes him dependent on the command staying this clean. If the walks creep up, there isn't enough swing-and-miss to cover for it, and the depth arm floor waits.

reports.name: Sterlin Thompson
reports.peak_summary: Projection: everyday regular with medium risk. The current bat shape is balanced over 214 PA.
reports.published_report: The .472 OBP is what you lead with, because everything else flows from a guy who walks 18% of the time at Triple-A while striking out only 17%. Translated to a major-league context, that walk rate becomes 12.8% against a baseline of 8.5%, and the strikeout rate actually ticks below average, so the approach isn't a Triple-A mirage. The power is the open question: six home runs in 214 PA, and the MLB-equivalent ISO of .139 sits just below the league mean, which means the everyday-regular ceiling requires either more loft or enough speed to keep defenses honest — he has 11 stolen bases, so that lever exists. If the bat-to-ball skill and patience hold at the big-league level, this is a legitimate everyday left fielder; if the power stays buried, he's a very useful platoon piece rather than a lineup fixture.

reports.name: Dillon Dingler
reports.published_report: The xSLG sits at .537 and the xBA at .294, both in the 95th-96th percentile range, yet his actual production has run well behind that contact quality — and the chase rate explains most of the gap. At 34.4%, he's chasing more than three quarters of the league, and the walk rate at 6.6% reflects that same lack of patience at the edges. The underlying contact when he does connect is genuine: 48.0% hard-hit, 11.9% barrel rate, the kind of shape that supports a .484 projected SLG even after the discipline discount. If the chase rate tightens even modestly, you've got a true middle-of-the-order catcher; if it doesn't, the projection of .259/.320/.484 with 28 home runs across 586 PA is probably the ceiling, not the floor.

reports.name: Chris Sale
reports.published_report: That 35.4% chase rate is the load-bearing number here. Sale gets hitters to chase at a clip that ranks in the 92nd percentile, and he pairs it with a 6.1% walk rate, which means the zone/chase mix is working the way it's supposed to, not leaking free passes on the edges. The strikeout rate sits at 28.6%, the hard-hit rate at 32.8% is well below the league middle, and those two figures together explain why the xwOBA (.289) and xERA (3.44) land comfortably better than average even as he plays his age-37 season. A projected 2.68 ERA implies he's outrunning those expected numbers, so the dependency is durability: 174.7 projected innings at 37, post-injuries, is the assumption everything else rests on, and if he can't hold that workload the gap between the ERA and what actually gets banked narrows fast.

reports.published_report: The strikeout rate translates well — his 11.2 K/9 at AAA/AA comes out to 9.0 in MLB-equivalent terms, nudging past the big-league mean of 8.6, and a K-BB% sitting at the 80th percentile among arms with meaningful innings suggests the miss is his most reliable carrying tool. The walks are the profile's load-bearing flaw: a translated 3.8 BB/9 sits above the MLB average of 3.2, and if command doesn't improve from that 50-grade shape, the ceiling compresses fast. Everything here points toward a multi-inning or setup role rather than rotation depth, the starter volume across 72 innings notwithstanding, and the floor if the walks drift further is a depth arm burning time in Triple-A. Carr is a useful MLB arm if the miss holds and the walks stabilize, and at 24 that's a reasonable outcome to bet on.

reports.published_report: The walk rate is the loudest thing in this profile. Fifty walks in 284 PA at AA, translating to a 12.6% BB rate against a major-league average around 8.5%, is the kind of approach that keeps a first baseman's floor from caving. The problem is the 31% strikeout rate at the level, which travels to roughly 30% against MLB pitching, and a first baseman who whiffs that often needs the power to be abundant and undeniable. reports.name: Cal Raleigh
reports.published_report:
The tension here is one number against everything else: an 11.3% barrel rate in the 73rd percentile, attached to a contact profile that's basically unusable. His xBA is .177, his chase rate is 36.8%, his whiff rate is 31.9%, and all three land in the bottom sixth of the league. The barrels show up in the barrel column specifically because he's squaring the ball when he does make contact, but they're marooned in a sea of swings and misses that depress everything around them.

What you're left with is a catcher who projects for 24 home runs in 519 plate appearances at a .191 average, which is the mathematical summary of what happens when elite bat-to-barrel skill meets elite bat-to-nothing everything else. His 12.2% walk rate saves the on-base line from total collapse. If the strikeout rate ever bends toward average, you have a legitimate run-producer behind the plate; if it doesn't, you have exactly what the .679 projected OPS says: a positional asset whose value lives almost entirely in the glove.

reports.name: Seiya Suzuki
reports.published_report: The profile is a contradiction: a 23.0% chase rate that ranks among the better marks in baseball, paired with a 26.5% strikeout rate that looks nothing like it. He's seeing the ball well enough to lay off, but when he swings he's whiffing at a 26.1% clip, and the contact itself lands right at league average across exit velocity, hard-hit rate, and xSLG. That's the tension in a nutshell. The walk rate at 10.7% keeps the OBP afloat and explains how a .246 xBA becomes a projected .342 OBP, but 24 projected home runs out of a bat with an 8.7% barrel rate and a .410 xSLG reads as a guy whose power is more volume than violence. He's a solid regular if the strikeout rate doesn't climb further; if it does, the whole profile leans on patience alone, and that's a thinner ledge than it looks.

reports.name: Sam Antonacci
reports.published_report: The xBA sitting at .296 (96th percentile) while average exit velocity checks in at 87.8 mph tells you almost everything about who Antonacci is: a contact artist who beats the ball into the ground and through gaps rather than lifting it over fences. His 22.3% chase rate and 15.7% whiff rate are genuine strengths, and the .366 xwOBA reflects a hitter who earns his way on base through plate discipline and bat-to-ball, not raw power. Nine projected home runs over 539 plate appearances, paired with a 7.1% walk rate that trails most of the league, means the whole offensive case rests on that contact quality holding, because if pitchers start living in the zone and daring him to do damage, the .396 SLG offers no threat to keep them honest. The 21 projected stolen bases give the profile real utility, and he fits cleanly as an everyday outfielder on a contender's bench or a low-end regular on a rebuilding club like Chicago, which he already is.
